content: Several studies compared HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) assays to nucleic acid testing (NAT) for assessing sustained virologic response (SVR). However, only descriptive analyses were feasible due to the lack of sufficient data for meta-analysis. Some studies focused on whether an early decline in HCVcAg could predict SVR and the optimal time for such predictions. These findings were described, but no studies using direct-acting antiviral (DAA) interferon-free regimens were included, limiting the applicability of the results to current DAA treatments. The review was conducted during a period of rapid advancements in the field, raising questions about the utility of viral load monitoring during treatment with highly effective therapies and the role of HCVcAg as a surrogate for NAT. Strengths of the review included the use of a predefined protocol for literature search, article selection, data extraction, and quality assessment. The search was unrestricted by language, but three articles in Russian, Korean, and Polish were excluded due to translation issues. Despite efforts to contact authors for missing data, some studies were excluded due to lack of response or inability to provide original data. Bivariate random-effects modeling was used when appropriate to derive pooled estimates, and univariate analyses were performed to maximize data utilization. Further research is needed to understand the outcomes of patients with low viral loads, including whether they are more likely to resolve their infection or experience disease progression warranting treatment. Similarly, more data are required on patients with high viral loads but negative HCVcAg results to optimize antigen detection. The kinetics of HCV RNA and HCVcAg during the pre-seroconversion phase and their correlation remain poorly understood. Additional studies are necessary to evaluate the impact of covariates such as HIV or HBV coinfection and HCV genotype on the accuracy of HCVcAg for diagnosing active infection and monitoring treatment outcomes. The kinetics of HCVcAg during treatment, particularly with new DAA regimens, also require further investigation. This systematic review demonstrated that several HCVcAg assays exhibit high sensitivity (>90%) and specificity (>98%) compared to NAT. While the sensitivity of HCVcAg does not match that of NAT, well-performing assays with analytical sensitivity in the femtomolar range (~3000 IU/mL) and diagnostic sensitivity of ~95% could serve as a replacement for NAT in HCV detection, especially if they are more cost-effective. HCVcAg tests could also be used as a one-step screening test, as they become positive earlier than antibody tests (1–2 days after HCV RNA appears) and have high specificity, eliminating the need for confirmatory testing. To expand access to testing in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), point-of-care (POC) tests with improved sample processing and transport mechanisms are needed. While HCVcAg tests are feasible on POC platforms, the need for signal amplification suggests that instrument-free assays are unlikely in the near future. The role of HCVcAg as a substitute for NAT in assessing SVR remains unclear. Although two studies showed excellent results, data on the early kinetics of HCVcAg and the optimal timing for SVR prediction are limited. Acknowledgments were extended to authors who provided additional data and individuals who assisted with translations, search terms, and technical aspects of HCVcAg tests.
